title: Spanning trees in the Assignment Problem: two theorems and two conjectures
authors: Sergio Caracciolo, Gabriele Sicuro, Andrea Sportiello
abstract: The \emph{Minimum Matching Problem} consists of finding an independent edge set of minimum weight $M_{\star}(G)$ in a given edge-weighted graph $G$. When $G$ is bipartite, this reduces to the \emph{Assignment Problem}. We consider a variant of this problem defined by taking the union of optimal matchings across various slightly modified versions of the base graph: $H_{\mathcal{J}}(G)=\bigcup_{U \in \mathcal{J}} M_{\star}(G_{U})$. We establish two families of results: (1) In two distinct settings for the Assignment Problem, we prove that the resulting graphs $H_{\mathcal{J}}$, as well as certain associated graphs $\bar{H}_{\mathcal{J}}$, are spanning trees on the relevant base graphs $G$ and $\bar{G}$. (2) In these same settings, assuming the edge weights are given by the $p$-th power of Euclidean distances for point configurations in the plane, we show that for $p=1$ the tree $H_{\mathcal{J}}$ is non-crossing (i.e., its planar embedding has no crossing edges), whereas, remarkably, for $p=2$ the associated tree $\bar{H}_{\mathcal{J}}$ is non-crossing. Finally, we introduce novel conjectures in Statistical Mechanics, to be explored in future work: in the Random Euclidean Assignment Problem (where points are i.i.d.\ on a planar domain), we conjecture that for $p=2$ the trees $\bar{H}_{\mathcal{J}}$ are asymptotically distributed as Uniform Spanning Trees with free and wired boundary conditions in the two respective settings. In particular, suitable paths on the tree in the second setting, and on its planar dual in the first setting, are asymptotically distributed as $\text{SLE}_κ$ with $κ=2$.
summary: This paper analyzes spanning trees derived from the Assignment Problem using geometric weights based on Euclidean distances. Key results prove that these structures are spanning trees and exhibit non-crossing properties for specific exponents ($p=1, 2$). The work culminates in conjectures linking these random graph structures to established concepts in statistical mechanics, such as Uniform Spanning Trees and $	ext{SLE}_\kappa$ curves.
main_problem: The paper investigates the structure of spanning trees derived from the Minimum Matching Problem, particularly when the graph is bipartite (the Assignment Problem). It extends this analysis to geometric settings using Euclidean distances.
main_result: The authors prove that the constructed graphs $H$ and $ ar{H}$ are spanning trees in specific settings, and they establish conditions under which these trees are non-crossing for $p=1$ and $p=2$. Furthermore, they conjecture an asymptotic connection to Uniform Spanning Trees and SLE curves.
method: The analysis combines combinatorial optimization (Minimum Matching/Assignment Problem) with geometric probability and continuum limits. Techniques involve analyzing cost matrices derived from Euclidean distances and comparing results on flat versus curved manifolds.
model_or_system: The model centers on finding optimal matchings in weighted graphs where weights are defined by the $p$-th power of Euclidean distances between point configurations in the plane. The context is generalized to random point configurations on planar domains or curved manifolds.
key_observables: The structure of the resulting graphs ($H$ and $ ar{H}$), the non-crossing property of their planar embeddings, and the asymptotic distribution of paths ($	ext{SLE}_\kappa$).
important_parameters: The exponent $p$ (especially $p=1$ and $p=2$), the curvature of the manifold ($\eta$), and the density/distribution of the point configurations.
main_assumptions: The theorems rely on 'suitable generality hypotheses.' The analysis of curved manifolds involves expansions in small parameters ($\eta$ and $	heta$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates an example showing that for $p=2$, the projected graph $ ar{H}$ is non-crossing, while the direct construction $H$ is crossing.
paper_structure: The paper establishes foundational theorems regarding the spanning tree nature of $H_{\mathcal{J}}$ and $ ar{H}_{\mathcal{J}}$. It then analyzes the geometric properties (non-crossing) for specific distance metrics ($p=1, 2$). Finally, it introduces conjectures concerning the asymptotic behavior of these trees in the Random Euclidean Assignment Problem, linking them to UST and SLE.
why_interesting: While the core is combinatorial optimization, the connection to geometric properties (non-crossing paths) and the explicit link to $	ext{SLE}_\kappa$ places this work at the intersection of statistical mechanics, random geometry, and critical phenomena, which is highly relevant to condensed matter theory.
